chapters.name: Chapter 1: Your message and your posts

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding your core marketing message
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write one or two sentences that say who you serve, what you do and why you are different.
This lesson builds toward: Using the core message formula and an AI assistant, you will write a core message that says who you serve, what you do and why you are different, in one or two true sentences that sound like you.
Your core message is the short answer to "Why should I choose you?" Every post, flyer and sign should repeat it in different words.
A simple formula: We help [who] get [what] with [what makes us different]. Example: "We help busy families in South Sacramento get home-style Filipino meals, ready in 10 minutes, made by the same family since 2009."
Ask AI to help you find it: "Here is what customers say about my shop and what I do differently. Write five versions of a one-sentence core message." Pick the one that sounds true and like you.
Step by step:
- Write who you serve.
- Write what they get.
- Write what makes you different (true, specific).
- Ask AI for five versions and pick one.
Words to know:
- Core message: the short statement of why customers should choose you.
- Differentiator: something true that makes you different from competitors.
Try it now: Fill in the formula for your business. Then ask an AI assistant for five versions and choose the best one.
You can now write a clear core message for your business.

check.q: What question does a core message answer for customers?
options: How many staff do you have?
Where did you buy your equipment?
check.why: A core message tells customers why to choose you.

check.q: AI gives you five core message versions, and the best one claims you are "the city's #1 salon". What would you do?
options: Use it because it sounds strong
Pick a version that is true and sounds like you
check.why: Your core message must be true and sound like you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing social posts and captions with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your core message into several social posts in your own voice.
This lesson builds toward: Given your core message, you will write social posts and captions with AI help, with a real detail added to each, nothing untrue, and permission for any customer photo.
Good small business posts show real things: today's special, a before-and-after haircut, a happy customer (with permission), your team, behind the scenes, a tip, an event. People follow people.
Ask AI for drafts: "Write four short Instagram captions for my barbershop. Core message: [your message]. One about our Saturday hours, one about a fade, one introducing our new barber Marcus, one with a hair care tip. Friendly, 2 sentences each, 3 hashtags."
Then edit. Add real details only you know. Remove anything that sounds fake or over the top. Always get permission before posting a customer's photo or name.
Step by step:
- Choose four post types: offer, behind the scenes, team, tip.
- Ask AI for captions with your core message and voice.
- Add real details and cut anything fake.
- Get permission for any customer photo or name.
Words to know:
- Caption: the text that goes with a social media photo or video.
- Hashtag: a word with # in front, used to group posts on a topic.
Try it now: Ask AI for four captions for your business with your core message. Edit each one to add a real detail and remove anything that is not true.
You can now write social posts with AI help that sound real and like your business.

options: The text with a social photo or video
check.why: A caption is the text that goes with your photo or video post.

check.q: You want to post a great photo of a customer's new haircut. What would you do first?
options: Ask AI if it is okay
check.why: You need the customer's permission before posting their photo.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Designing a flyer or promo graphic
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a clear flyer or graphic for one offer or event.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free design tool, you will make a flyer for one offer or event, with a headline, one real picture, three details and a call to action, all checked.
A flyer works on a counter, a community board, a church bulletin or as a social post. Use a free design tool like Canva or Adobe Express, starting from a template.
Keep the parts clear: a big headline (the offer), one picture, three short details (what, when, where), and a call to action ("Call to book", "Order online"). Use your core message in small words at the bottom.
If you use AI-generated images, make sure they do not show food, work or results you do not really offer. Use your own photos when you can; customers trust real pictures.
Step by step:
- Open a design tool and choose a template.
- Write a big headline with the offer.
- Add one picture, three details and a call to action.
- Check spelling, phone number, date and address.
- Download or share.
Words to know:
- Call to action: the words that tell people what to do next, like "Call to book".
- Headline: the biggest words on a flyer or ad.
Try it now: Make a flyer for one real offer or event with a headline, one picture, three details and a call to action. Check every detail before you save it.
You can now design a clear flyer or promo graphic for your business.

check.q: What is a call to action?
options: A phone call to a customer
Words telling people what to do next
check.why: A call to action tells people the next step, like "Call to book".

check.q: Your flyer has an AI picture of a cake you do not make. What would you do?
options: Keep it because it looks nice
Add a note saying it is AI
Replace it with a real photo of what you sell
check.why: Pictures should show what you really sell.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Planning a monthly content calendar
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan four weeks of posts in a simple calendar.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and a table, you will plan a four-week content calendar, with a number of posts you can keep up, a mix of post types and every date checked.
A content calendar is a table that says what you will post and when. It stops the "what do I post today?" panic.
Make columns: Date, Platform, Post type, Idea, Caption done?, Picture done?. Plan two or three posts a week you can really keep up. Mix types: offers, tips, team, customers (with permission), and community events.
Ask AI: "Make a four-week posting calendar for my cleaning business, two posts a week, mixing offers, tips and team posts. Our core message is [...]. Include holidays and local events in [city] in [month] I should check." Then check each date and event yourself.
Step by step:
- Make a calendar table with six columns.
- Choose how many posts a week you can keep up.
- Ask AI for four weeks of ideas.
- Check dates and local events yourself.
- Mark posts done as you go.
Words to know:
- Content calendar: a schedule of what you will post and when.
- Platform: a social media site or app, like Instagram, Facebook or TikTok.
Try it now: Ask AI for a four-week, two-posts-a-week calendar for your business. Put it in a table and check every date.
You can now plan a month of posts in a content calendar.

options: A schedule of what you post and when
check.why: A content calendar plans your posts by date.

check.q: AI's calendar plans two posts every day, but you have time for two a week. What would you do?
options: Try to post every day anyway
Cut it to a number you can really keep up
check.why: Plan a number of posts you can really keep up.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Keeping your marketing honest and legal
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your marketing for claims you cannot back up, fake reviews and email rules.
This lesson builds toward: Given your captions and flyer, you will check your marketing for claims you cannot prove, fake reviews and email rules, with every unproven claim changed or removed.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says advertising must be truthful and not misleading, and you need proof for claims you make. "Best tacos in LA" reads as opinion, but "Our cleaning kills 99% of germs" or "Lose 10 pounds" is a claim you must be able to back up.
AI likes big words: "guaranteed", "award-winning", "number one". Remove any you cannot prove. Never post fake reviews or testimonials; the FTC's review rule bans them, including ones written by AI.
Marketing emails must follow CAN-SPAM: honest sender and subject, say it is an ad, include your postal address and an easy unsubscribe, and honor unsubscribes within 10 business days.
Step by step:
- Underline every claim in your post or flyer.
- Ask: can I prove this?
- Remove or change claims you cannot prove.
- No fake reviews or testimonials.
- Check marketing emails for CAN-SPAM basics.
Words to know:
- Claim: a statement of fact in an ad, like "kills 99% of germs".
- Misleading: likely to give people a wrong idea.
- Testimonial: a customer's statement praising your business, used in marketing.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing basics
- FTC: Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule, Questions and Answers
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act, A Compliance Guide for Business
Try it now: Take your four captions and your flyer. Underline every claim, and change or remove any you cannot prove.
You can now check your marketing for unprovable claims, fake reviews and email rule problems.

check.q: According to the FTC, what must ads be?
check.why: FTC rules say ads must be truthful and not misleading.

check.q: AI wrote "Voted best tacos in LA" in your caption, but no vote happened. What would you do?
options: Change it to "Voted best tacos in town"
check.why: Claims you cannot prove must be removed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Seeing what works
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track which posts and flyers bring in customers.
This lesson builds toward: Given your posts and flyer, you will create a tracking table that shows which marketing brings in customers, with a promo code on one offer and any AI pattern confirmed in the table.
Likes are nice, but customers matter more. Track simple signals: messages and calls, bookings, people who mention a post, and use of a special code ("Say FLYER10 for 10% off").
Most social platforms show free numbers for business accounts, such as reach and profile visits; look for the insights or analytics section. Write the key numbers in a tracking table each week.
Once a month, paste your table (no customer names) into an AI assistant and ask: "Which post types brought the most bookings? What should I do more of?" Confirm it in your table, then plan next month.
Step by step:
- Choose signals: messages, bookings, mentions, code use.
- Add a special code to one offer.
- Record the numbers weekly in a table.
- Ask AI for patterns once a month and confirm them.
Words to know:
- Reach: how many people saw a post.
- Insights: the numbers a platform shows about how your posts did.
- Promo code: a word customers say or type to get an offer, which helps you track it.
Try it now: Final task: finish your month of marketing: core message, four-week calendar, four finished captions, one flyer, and a tracking table with a promo code on one offer. Check every claim and image.
You can now plan, make and measure a month of honest marketing for your business.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Core message Vague, or says something untrue. One or two true sentences: who you serve, what you do, why you are different. It appears in the posts and the flyer. Content calendar Fewer than eight posts, or dates not checked. Four weeks with at least eight posts, dates checked. Mixes offers, tips, team and community posts. Captions Fewer than four, or they contain untrue details. Four finished captions with a real detail in each. Each has a clear call to action and sounds like the owner. Flyer Missing a headline, details or call to action. Headline, one real picture, three details and a call to action, all checked. Includes a promo code for tracking. Honest claims and images A claim cannot be proven, or an image is not yours to use. Every claim can be proven and every image is yours or used with permission. The owner can say how each claim is backed up. Tracking table No way to tell which posts worked. A table to record results, with a promo code on one offer. Uses free insights numbers and plans to review results at the end of the month. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: How many people saw a post
check.why: Reach is the number of people who saw a post.

check.q: You want to know if your flyer brought in customers. What would you do?
options: Guess from how busy it feels
Put a special promo code on the flyer and track it
check.why: A special code shows which marketing brought each customer.
